system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2141-10-14 03:55:00 to 2141-10-19 18:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with altered mental status and respiratory failure following a drug overdose involving benzodiazepines, opiates, and cocaine. He was intubated for airway protection and managed in the ICU with supportive care, including IV hydralazine for hypertension and antibiotics for suspected UTI. Toxicology and psychiatry consultations indicated a non-suicidal mixed ingestion. He was successfully extubated on hospital day two, completed a course of antibiotics, and stabilized medically. His chronic conditions, including CKD, neurogenic bladder, and seizure disorder, were managed without complication. He was discharged home with simplified medications, a short course of oral nitrofurantoin, and referrals for psychiatry, substance use counseling, and primary care follow-up.

Combinations of opioid type drug with any other drug dependence, continuous
Cauda equina syndrome with neurogenic bladder
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage I through stage IV, or unspecified

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ with T12 paraplegia, multiple right lower extremity
fractures.  Please evaluate for deep vein thrombosis.

COMPARISON:  No prior studies available for comparison.

FINDINGS:  Exam is severely limited due to patient's paraplegia, contracted
left lower extremity and multiple right lower extremity fractures and
overlying splint.

In the left lower extremity, the common femoral and proximal superficial
femoral veins were the only vessels able to be evaluated and they demonstrate
normal compressibility, flow, and augmentation.

In the right lower extremity, the right common femoral, superficial femoral,
and popliteal veins were assessed and demonstrate normal compressibility, flow
and augmentation throughout.

IMPRESSION:  Limited exam.  No deep vein thrombosis identified in the left
common femoral and proximal superficial femoral veins nor in the right common
femoral through popliteal veins.

INDICATION:  Preoperative evaluation.

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to chest radiograph performed ___.

FINDINGS:  AP and lateral radiograph demonstrates unremarkable mediastinal,
hilar and cardiac contours.  Low lung volumes are noted bilaterally with
resultant crowding of the vasculature structures.  No overt pulmonary edema
evident.  No pleural effusion or pneumothorax evident.  Thoracic vertebral
stabilization devices are again noted.

IMPRESSION:  No acute intrathoracic process.

INDICATION:  Fracture status post reduction and realignment.  Please evaluate.

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to tib-fib radiographs performed ___.

FINDINGS:  Redemonstration of the minimally displaced obliquely oriented
fracture through the proximal aspect of the tibia and fibula with slight
improved alignment.  Small joint effusion noted.  Significant soft tissue
swelling is present overlying knee and fracture site.

IMPRESSION:  Slightly improved alignment of the minimally displaced fracture
of the proximal tibia and fibula. Small joint effusion.

HISTORY:  Status post fall with right intertrochanteric and tibiofibular
fracture.  Evaluate for pelvic or hip fracture.  The patient is paraplegic;
status post fall.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen and pelvis ___, right tibia-fibula
___ and right femur and right knee ___.

TECHNIQUE:  AP pelvis, single view.

FINDINGS:  There is similar dislocation of the left femoral head superiorly
and posteriorly in relation to the acetabulum.  Severe degenerative changes
are seen in bilateral hip joints.  The known right  greater trochanteric
fracture is less apparent on current view.  Lucency with sclerosis in the left
iliac wing is similar, likely bone donor site.  Partially imaged hardware is
seen at the lower lumbar spine.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Similar dislocation of the left femoral head superior and posterior in
relation to the acetabulum.
2.  Right greater trochanteric fracture.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  Right proximal tibia fracture in cast.

RIGHT TIBIA AND FIBULA, FOUR FILMS.

Following casting the alignment of the fractured tibia and fibula is unchanged
since the prior films and appears satisfactory.  Alignment of ankle appears
normal.

HISTORY:  Fracture postop casting.

AP view of the femur plus lateral of distal femur.  No lateral or the proximal
femur was obtained.  

Detail is considerably obscured by the overlying cast. There is a fracture of
the proximal tibia, with slight lateral displacement of the distal fragment
and lateral apex angulation.  Possible proximal fibular fracture.    There
does appear to be a knee joint effusion, with fat-fluid level. There is
irregularity of the greater trochanter of the proximal femur and patchy
density in this area, as well, of uncertain significance.  There is background
diffuse osteopenia, much greater than expected in someone of this age.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, I’m Dr. ___ from Orthopedics. You were brought in after a fall from your wheelchair four days ago. We’ve reviewed your X-rays and found fractures in your right hip and leg. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m in a lot of pain, especially in my right leg. I didn’t think it was this bad when it happened, but the swelling got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve started you on pain medication to help. The X-rays show a fracture near your hip — that’s called an intertrochanteric femur fracture — and another in your tibia and fibula, the bones in your lower leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery? I’m worried about complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed that with the team. Because you’re already non-weight-bearing due to your paraplegia, and because of your other health conditions, the risks of surgery outweigh the benefits. We’re treating this non-operatively with bracing and careful monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But will the bones heal properly without surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may take longer, but with proper immobilization and care, they can heal. We’ve already done a closed reduction in the ER to realign the bones, and the follow-up X-ray shows improved alignment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my UTI? My primary doctor just started me on Augmentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing that. You have a history of recurrent UTIs, so we want to make sure this one clears up. We’ll keep you on the amoxicillin-clavulanate, which is similar to Augmentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had bad reactions to some antibiotics before. I’m allergic to Bactrim and Cipro.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ve reviewed your allergies — you’re allergic to Bactrim, Levaquin, Vancomycin, and several others. We’ll avoid those completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. And my seizures — I take levetiracetam regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued your levetiracetam. No seizure activity noted since admission. We’ll keep that up to prevent any episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been anxious lately. Is it okay if I keep taking my anxiety meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added alprazolam to your discharge plan for anxiety, as needed. We’ll monitor how you’re doing, but it’s safe to use with your other medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate that. What about blood clots? I’ve heard that’s a risk when you can’t move much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent point. We did an ultrasound to check for deep vein thrombosis. The results were negative — no clots found in your legs. But to prevent any from forming, we’re starting enoxaparin, a blood thinner, for four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to give that to myself? I can’t feel my legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a daily injection under the skin. A home health nurse will come to help you with it, and train your caregiver if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. What about my kidney? I have CKD, and some meds can hurt it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that closely. Your baseline creatinine is known, and we’ve adjusted your sevelamer dose accordingly. We’re avoiding any nephrotoxic drugs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my pain meds — I was on oxycodone before. Is that still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adjusting your pain regimen. You’ll be on a lower-dose extended-release oxycodone, plus a smaller dose as needed. We’re being cautious due to your history and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I don’t want to overdo it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I wanted to update you — we repeated the X-rays after casting, and the alignment of your tibia and fibula is stable. No changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the brace supposed to stay on all the time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it must stay locked in extension at all times. You should not remove it. Also, check the skin under the brace daily — we don’t want pressure sores, especially with your history of MRSA ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I’ll have my mom help with that. She’s been managing my care for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll also have a home health nurse visit to assist with wound checks and injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’ve been feeling a bit anxious about going home. Will I be able to manage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re setting you up with home health services, physical therapy, and nursing support. You’ll have help with meds, injections, and mobility. And you’re going home with a new wheelchair with elevating leg rests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. Can I sit up in the wheelchair?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can be out of bed in the wheelchair with assistance. But you must remain non-weight-bearing on the right leg. Keep it elevated to reduce swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No walking on it — not that I could anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is better controlled now, and your swelling is improving. We’re planning for discharge in the next couple of days if everything stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What meds will I be going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue docusate and senna for bowel management, levetiracetam for seizures, pantoprazole for stomach protection, and amlodipine for blood pressure. Plus the enoxaparin, antibiotics, and pain meds we discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sleep? I’ve been using Ambien.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to zolpidem, which is similar, and also allowing trazodone or clonazepam as needed. We want to minimize sedatives but help you rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I saw the X-ray report mentioned a joint effusion. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means there’s some fluid in the knee joint, likely from the injury. It’s not unusual and should resolve as the fracture heals. We’re watching it, but no intervention is needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the osteopenia mentioned — is that related to my paraplegia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, prolonged immobility can lead to bone thinning. That’s why healing may take longer. We’ll discuss long-term bone health with your primary doctor later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re being discharged today. You’re in stable condition, pain is controlled, and your fractures are stable without surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the brace on, elevate your leg, don’t bear weight, and check your skin daily. Continue all meds, especially the enoxaparin for four weeks. Avoid alcohol and driving while on narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see orthopedics in two weeks. Physical therapy will start at home. Call us if you develop fever, redness, increased pain, or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, follow the instructions, and you’ll do well. The home health team will be there this afternoon.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted following a fall from his wheelchair four days prior, resulting in a right intertrochanteric femur fracture and right tibia/fibula fracture. Given his baseline paraplegia and comorbidities, non-operative management with bracing was chosen over surgery. He received closed reduction in the emergency department, with stable alignment confirmed on follow-up imaging. His pain was well controlled, and he engaged in physical therapy while in the hospital. A concurrent urinary tract infection was treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate. He remained neurologically stable, with no complications during his stay. He was discharged home with home health services, a new wheelchair, and detailed instructions for non-weight-bearing status, skin care, anticoagulation, and medication management.

Other and unspecified alcohol dependence, in remission
